rationale: "Borrowing limits" is a <div class="h2"> styled to look like a heading. Sighted readers see a heading; the accessibility tree contains no heading at all, so the page has zero headings and cannot be navigated by heading — the primary way screen-reader users move through a long document. The visual hierarchy is real and the programmatic one is absent, which is exactly what 1.3.1 forbids.

"Borrowing limits" is a real <h2>. The structure a sighted reader sees is written into the markup, so heading navigation works. Note this element is correctly NOT selected by the semantics rule — a native heading with no overriding role has real semantics and needs no judgment — so it is expected to score as never-looked-at rather than as a verdict.

A table built out of <div class="grid-row">. It reads as a three-column table of loans to anyone who can see it, and to a screen reader it is an undifferentiated run of text with no column headers, no row boundaries and no count. A cell's value cannot be associated with the column it belongs to, so "14 March" is announced with no indication of whether it is the borrowed or the returned date.

The same data as a real <table> with three <th scope="col"> header cells. Each value is programmatically associated with its column, so a screen reader announces "Returned, 14 March" rather than a bare date.

Three radio buttons that each carry a correct individual <label>, inside a form with no fieldset and no legend. Every rule-level check passes: no input is unlabelled. What is missing is the relationship — nothing says these three options belong to one question, so a screen reader announces "Email, radio button, 1 of 3" with no statement of what is being chosen. The visible <h2> "Notify me by" supplies that to a sighted reader only.
The same three radios inside a <fieldset> with a <legend>. The group has a programmatic name, so each option is announced in the context of the question it answers.

A real <table> whose five header cells are <td>, styled to look like headers (uppercase, bold, tinted background) but carrying no <th> and no scope. The table has seven body rows and five columns, so a value in the fourth column is announced as a bare number with nothing to say it means "Available". This is the case that motivated the `structure` checker: the table is not pretending to be anything, so the `semantics` rule never reaches it, and every page of the 21 August audit was recorded as satisfying 1.3.1 with its tables unexamined.
The same table with five <th scope="col"> header cells and the same seven body rows. Identical to the eye, correct in the tree.
